results.title: I put Linux on Microsoft’s own hardware, and it somehow works so much better than Windows
results.author: Amir Bohlooli
results.content:
You've heard the advice. I have too. In fact, I've even given it. Heck, I've even followed said advice, on numerous occasions. What advice? Ah, yes. The "just install Linux" advice.
I had a Dell Latitude that I bought used. It came with Windows 10, then spent some time as a headless Ubuntu server, and when I eventually built a proper homelab, I installed Ubuntu Desktop on it instead. It works so, so smoothly.
That successful installation was still lingering in the back of my head when I saw an old Microsoft Surface Pro 6 lying around. It's my dad's, and he mainly uses it as a tablet with the Surface Pen for writing.
The problem was that this Microsoft device could barely hold a charge, got ridiculously hot, and was laggy all the time. Windows just wasn't working particularly well on this Surface. So... can we put Linux on a Microsoft Surface? A device that was literally made for Windows?
Yes, you can put Linux on a Surface
"You can install Linux on anything"
Of course you can. The more nuanced question is whether everything will actually work afterward.
I'll spare you the platitude, but Linux really has come a long way. After all, the year of the Linux desktop is coming (any day now!) We've even got gamers, of all people, switching to Linux on their PCs. So why not a Surface?
A Surface packs quite a bit of hardware that falls outside what you'd expect from an ordinary laptop: there's a touchscreen. There are two cameras, in addition to the Windows Hello IR camera. There's the Surface Pen. Depending on the model, there are all sorts of sensors and other Microsoft-specific hardware to worry about.
|  | 
| A cute message I got from the Surface Pro as I was very vigorously trying to shut it down. | 
Some hardware simply does not work properly on Linux. But lo and behold, there's an entire project dedicated to making Linux work on Surface devices.
Linux-surface provides a customized kernel and drivers to get Surface hardware running properly under Linux. In theory, you can install just about any distro on a Surface, set up linux-surface, and start tinkering. In practice, the project provides straightforward installation instructions for the usual mainstream distros: buntu, Debian, Fedora, and Arch-based systems.
So, install a distro, set up linux-surface, fiddle with whatever breaks, and eventually I should have a working Linux Surface. But I wanted it even easier. Could it get easier?
Ultramarine basically does the work for you
Thankfully, we're not the first people to want this
Take roughly what Linux Mint does for Ubuntu and apply that philosophy to Fedora. You get something along the lines of Ultramarine Linux.
It's essentially Fedora with a bunch of useful extras already baked in. More importantly for me, Ultramarine offers a Surface image that already includes linux-surface and the extra drivers and codecs needed for Microsoft's hardware.
You can download the image from Ultramarine's website. It comes with four desktop environments: KDE Plasma, Xfce, Budgie, and GNOME. I went with KDE Plasma.
The installation is, thanks to the wonderful age of GUI installers, very simple and straightforward. Getting the live USB to actually boot was a little less straightforward.
Secure Boot had other plans
The first time I booted from the USB, I got GRUB (great!) Then I selected Ultramarine and immediately got an error saying the kernel was missing (not great!)
The problem, as you may have guessed, was Secure Boot. I went into the Surface's UEFI settings, disabled Secure Boot, and tried booting the USB again. This time, instead of Linux, I got a blue screen demanding my BitLocker recovery key (also not great!)
I had completely forgotten about Windows device encryption. This Surface Pro 6 had been running Windows 11 Home, where encryption can be enabled automatically without you knowing.
Fortunately, the fix was more annoying than difficult. I grabbed the recovery key from my Microsoft account, typed in the 48 digits, changed the boot order so I could get back into Windows, suspended the encryption protection from PowerShell, and rebooted.
I say "suspended" because fully decrypting the drive would have taken considerably longer. And in this case, there wasn't much point. The next time this Surface booted from its SSD, Windows wasn't going to be there anymore anyway. After that, Ultramarine finally booted.
Linux made the Surface chill out
Most of the important stuff just works
Speakers, touchscreen, microphone, and cameras all worked immediately. Not a single terminal command was required to get any of them working. The Surface Pen connected and worked too, which was especially important considering that's basically the whole reason my dad uses this thing.
This sounds like the setup for me to now list everything that didn't work. Well... it is.
Alas, the Windows Hello IR camera does not work! I'm not even going to bother fighting that battle. It's a sacrifice I'm OK with. The regular cameras also aren't exactly perfect. The image is very dark and clearly needs some tuning. But hey, this is Linux we're talking about. I can dig into the configuration and tweak it however I like. Even make it look better than Windows Camera did.
The important peripherals work, though, and the difference was soon noticeable. The Surface runs much cooler now. I haven't heard the fan spin up once since switching to Linux, whereas Windows would make them run minutes after boot.
I'll eventually install my usual collection of open-source software and it'll start feeling like home pretty quickly. There is, however, one area where Windows still has the advantage.
Windows still knows it's a tablet
KDE isn't quite there yet
I've complained plenty in the past about Microsoft seemingly optimizing Windows 11 for an imaginary audience of tablet users. Well, ladies and gentlemen, I found the tablet user. It's me.
All that extra spacing, padding, oversized buttons, and touch-friendly UI suddenly makes much more sense when you're actually using Windows 11 on a touchscreen without a keyboard attached.
KDE Plasma does an OK job here. The on-screen keyboard pops up when I need it, and basic touch navigation works well enough. But it isn't elegant. The interface doesn't transform when I detach the Type Cover. There's no convincing equivalent of Windows recognizing that it's suddenly a tablet and adapting itself accordingly.
You can definitely use KDE with touch. I have been. But, it will still feel like operating a desktop interface with fingers rather than using an interface designed around them. That's probably the biggest compromise I've found so far.
I expected a project, not an upgrade
I went into this expecting Linux on a Surface Pro to be one of those fun (?) weekend projects. You know, the ones where you spend six hours fixing drivers, get 80% of the hardware working, declare victory, and then reinstall Windows three days later... That isn't what happened.
Ultramarine booted, the important Surface hardware worked, the Pen worked, and the machine became cooler and noticeably more pleasant to use. Even the pressure input from the pen worked. The biggest issue I've run into wasn't the kernel, which in itself is a blessing. It's that KDE isn't quite as comfortable on a tablet as Windows 11. That's a remarkably good problem to have. I have an array of Linux environments to choose from.
I wouldn't tell every Surface owner to immediately wipe Windows and install Linux. Windows still has better integration with some of the hardware, especially if things like Windows Hello and a polished tablet UI matter to you.
But if you've got an older Surface that's getting hot, sluggish, and increasingly unpleasant to use, I wouldn't write the hardware off just yet.
The solution to my aging Microsoft tablet was exactly the same nearly annoying advice everyone drops in the comments sections: just install Linux, bro.
results.summary:
Installing Ultramarine Linux on an aging Microsoft Surface Pro 6 improves thermal performance and system responsiveness, offering a viable alternative to Windows for users with older, sluggish hardware.

### Key Points
- The linux-surface project provides a customized kernel and drivers to ensure compatibility between Microsoft hardware and various Linux distributions.
- Ultramarine Linux offers a pre-configured installation image that includes the necessary drivers and codecs for Surface devices, simplifying the setup process.
- Essential hardware, including the touchscreen, speakers, microphone, and Surface Pen, functions immediately upon installation without requiring manual terminal configuration.
- Users must disable Secure Boot and manage BitLocker encryption keys within the UEFI settings to successfully boot from external installation media.
- While performance is improved, the Windows Hello IR camera remains unsupported, and desktop environments like KDE Plasma lack the native tablet-mode optimizations found in Windows 11.

### Why it Matters
Transitioning older Surface devices to Linux can extend the hardware's lifespan by reducing thermal output and eliminating the performance lag often associated with aging Windows installations. While users may sacrifice specific proprietary features like Windows Hello, the improved system stability provides a practical solution for those looking to repurpose legacy tablets.

results.title: Media Briefing: What to expect at the Digiday Publishing Summit, September 2026 edition
results.author: Sara Guaglione
results.content:
This Media Briefing covers the latest in media trends for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Thursday at 10 a.m. ET. More from the series →
This week’s Media Briefing covers what to expect from the upcoming Digiday Publishing Summit in Key Biscayne, Fla., which kicks off on Sept. 14. Executives from The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, Reuters, CNBC, USA Today Co., Politico will take the stage to unpack how the traditional publishing model is being rewritten to prepare for a world with fewer clicks and a shrinking open web.
- What to expect at DPS
- Why brands are turning to older creators for authenticity AI can’t fake
What to expect at DPS
When not holding a cocktail underneath swaying palm trees or taking a cool dip in the pool by the ocean, publishing execs will compare strategies, trade insights and confront shared challenges at the three-day Digiday Publishing Summit – all to figure out what comes next for publishing in the AI era.
Many of those challenges are existential. Audiences are increasingly getting information from AI-generated summaries and video feeds. Bots are scraping more publisher content, often without reciprocal compensation. Media companies are being forced to rethink how they reach audiences and make money.
Publishing execs will share how they’re adapting their businesses, as the old playbook loses its grip. The town halls will offer a cathartic platform for publishers to air their wins and their grievances under Chatham House rules (insights can be reported, but all are anonymously sourced).
We’ll offer more in-depth recaps of what was said onstage and behind closed doors in the coming weeks. For now, here’s a sneak peek of what to expect – for those attending, and for those we’ll miss – below.
Rebuilding the publishing model
The conversations onstage and off will carry forward what was discussed at the last Digiday Publishing Summit in Vail in March: publishers are redefining revenue in the AI era, through a mixture of subscriptions, AI content licensing, video production, and ad revenue operations. They’re determining how to reach their audiences beyond search, through video platforms, AI answer engines and product improvements, as AI reshapes how content is created, discovered and consumed.
Expect “GEO” and “AI visibility” to be buzzwords at the summit. In Vail, Time’s chief operating officer Mark Howard outlined how the publisher was pitching its GEO insights and AI visibility to brands.
At this month’s event, execs will explain how this area has evolved. Jacquelyn Cameron, CRO at Axios, will discuss onstage exploring new business opportunities to leverage AI visibility, such as through brand partnerships. Mike Peralta, CRO at Future, will unpack the strategies the publisher is using to stay visible in AI search engines, and how to capitalize on this while also trying to snag more AI licensing deals.
Redefining publisher revenue
As the economics of traffic and scale shift (and traffic-based monetization becomes less dependable), publishers are building a more diversified revenue mix spanning subscriptions, licensing, advertising and partnerships.
Phil Andraos, gm for digital at Reuters, will detail how the publisher is delicately balancing its push into a subscription business while continuing to grow its robust advertising business. Kristin Roberts, president of USA Today Media, will discuss where the company sees investment opportunities, ranging from AI product development to subscription offerings.
The old publishing model was built around scale: more traffic meant more impressions, which meant more ad revenue. But Reuters is betting that equation is changing. Attracting high-quality users, building direct relationships with them and using first-party data to make those audiences more valuable — both as potential subscribers and to advertisers – creates a model where subscriptions and advertising don’t have to compete for the same audience. A growing base of logged-in, highly engaged subscribers can strengthen both sides of the business, Andraos said in a recent interview.
Adam Greenberg, vp of strategic partnerships at The New York Times, will level set on the current AI licensing landscape, addressing where the momentum is (and isn’t) and how he’s weeding out the real revenue opportunities from the ones still in a nascent stage. Publishers shouldn’t assume that today’s AI business models are inevitable — or chase licensing dollars at the expense of their core businesses, he told Digiday.
“The dollars and cents aren’t very good right now for most — even those that got deals. It’ll be very interesting to see… what happens with all these early deals and renewals and how those models shift,” Greenberg said.
Rewiring audience growth and distribution
With search referrals under pressure and audiences increasingly fragmented, publishers are finding new ways to reach people, build habits and deepen direct relationships. Expect another big topic of conversation at DPS to be around “Google Zero,” and what may push publishers to finally block Google’s crawlers and risk losing valuable search traffic.
“The arrangement that governed the web that everybody was OK with… the quid pro quo that we will let you crawl our site and in return you give us traffic? That has greatly changed and no one had a conversation about it [first],” said Steve Horowitz, president of Ziff Davis’ tech & shopping business.
In his onstage session, Horowitz will share the publisher’s playbook for lessening its reliance on Google search traffic. He’ll outline how investments in video, social and newsletters have helped create new paths to growth and monetization.
Francesca Barber, Politico’s evp of product, audience and AI, will preview a new product rolling out this fall for both free and paid audiences to build loyalty and habitual behavior.
And Taneth Evans, head of digital at The Wall Street Journal, will talk onstage about the publisher’s push to produce more reporter-led video, social, audio and newsletters, and how this has helped reach new audiences, deepen engagement and drive subscriptions and revenue across its own platforms.
What we’ve heard
“It’s more than just ‘the publisher can’t opt out,’ and I think that’s critical to the plaintiff arguments from Penske and Chegg. It’s actually anti‑competitive against this nascent emerging AI market because the publishers can opt out of all these other [AI] companies, and they’re going to have to pay to license the content, and Google doesn’t have to because the publishers can’t opt out, and they just force the rights into the bundle.” 
– Jason Kint, CEO of Digital Content Next, on why the Penske v. Google goes beyond opt-outs.
Numbers to know
3 out of 10: guest op-eds submitted to The Wall Street Journal, The Washington Post and The New York Times, were labeled as at least 80%, per AI detector Pangram.
85,000: The number of subscribers The Onion currently has.
$2 million: The amount of annual recurring revenue ghost creator platform Virelox made last year.
60: The number of podcasts Netflix now has available on its platform.
What we’ve covered
Why brands are turning to older creators for authenticity AI can’t fake
- Millennial and Gen X creators bring mortgages, burnout, parenting, health scares, and mid-career pivots into their feeds: real-life problems that are hard to fake and increasingly valuable to brands looking for credibility with older, higher-spending audiences.
- Brands are noticing, and responding by building actual long-term relationships instead of one-off campaigns.
Read more here.
How every major platform pays creators
- Every major social platform now runs its own creator payout scheme, each with markedly different rules, structures and eligibility requirements.
- Here’s a breakdown of the monetization rules and requirements for Instagram, YouTube, TikTok, Twitch, X, Facebook, and Snap.
Read more here.
Creator industry admits that fee pricing is out of control, but can’t agree on a fix
- Half of marketers misprice creator fees and 40% of them believe they overpaid, per 1,000 marketing and procurement leaders surveyed by Billion Dollar Boy.
- Brands pay too much 90% of the time, which is creating an expectation problem, according to agency sources.
Read more here. 
The Telegraph’s next podcast play: video, events and paid memberships
- Fresh off its acquisition by Axel Springer, The Telegraph is pushing its podcast ambitions beyond audio.
- The publisher is building repeatable franchises that can span video, live events and paid membership, to further deepen direct relationships with audiences.
Read more here. 
The case for and against the ‘programmatic-ification’ of the creator economy
- Marketers have been trying to get influencer and creator marketing down to a science. There’s an efficiency play in these AI dashboards, agencies say.
- On the flip side: As marketers hand over more of the influencer and creator marketing playbook to automated tools, they run the risk of recreating programmatic’s pitfalls.
Read more here.
What we’re reading
The Saturday Evening Post, which has long chronicled American life, will publish its final print issue in January. President and publisher Joan SerVaas told the magazine’s 50,000 subscribers this was due to rising production costs, declining ad revenue and shifting reader habits.
Axel Springer has acquired The Circuit, an Abu Dhabi-based publication focused on tech and business in the region, where political instability, oil money and fast-rising tech, finance and entertainment industries are playing an ever bigger role in shaping the global narratives.
Hollywood studios have sued over AI. Now Google is courting them to use its tools
Google has been in talks with Disney, Universal, Warner Bros., Discovery and other studios about licensing their characters and film catalogs for its AI products, though thorny legal issues have slowed progress. No deals have been inked yet.
The SPJ has proposed new revisions to its code of ethics for the first time in 12 years, to cater for how news consumption is evolving.
Simon is letting brands target shoppers in its malls in other environments and use new measurement tools based on Simon’s consumer data.
Millennial and Gen X content creators offer consistency, authenticity, and storytelling; three things brands need now more than ever.
The Telegraph is expanding its video podcast strategy into franchises spanning events and paid memberships to deepen audience relationships.
results.summary:
The Digiday Publishing Summit in Key Biscayne, Florida, gathers media executives to discuss strategies for navigating the evolving publishing landscape amid the rise of AI and shifting traffic models.

### Key Points
- The summit features leaders from The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, Reuters, and Politico discussing the transition away from traditional traffic-based revenue models.
- Key topics include "GEO" (Generative Engine Optimization), AI visibility, and the development of diversified revenue streams through subscriptions, licensing, and brand partnerships.
- Executives are addressing the existential threat of AI-generated search summaries and the potential for publishers to block Google crawlers to protect content value.
- Industry experts are evaluating the current AI licensing landscape, noting that early financial returns for publishers remain inconsistent and nascent.
- Publishers are prioritizing direct audience relationships through newsletters, video, and social platforms to reduce reliance on search engine referrals.

### Why it Matters
The traditional publishing business model, long dependent on search-driven scale and ad impressions, is facing an existential crisis due to AI-driven content consumption. These discussions highlight a critical industry pivot toward high-quality, direct-to-consumer relationships and diversified revenue streams to ensure long-term financial viability.

results.title: Burnham to tackle 'mega-donors' in UK politics, minister says
results.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
results.content:
- Published
Andy Burnham's government is "determined to tackle" the issue of "mega-donors" in UK politics, a minister has said in response to calls for an immediate cap on donations.
Florence Eshalomi said a new team would be "working at pace to find a solution", as some MPs expressed concerns over the influence of wealthy individuals donating large sums of money.
The Labour government has already committed to a £100,000 annual cap on donations from British citizens living overseas, but ministers have been pressed to go further by introducing a limit for UK-based donors.
Reform UK's Danny Kruger warned the Representation of the People Bill was a "flagrantly partisan attempt to kneecap" the party.
Reform has been critical of measures contained in the bill and the impact they could have on funding the party receives from donors.
There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties and politicians.
Labour MP Stella Creasy said donations from individuals and companies giving £1m or more had "surged" in the last decade and gave examples for different political parties.
Among those she named was British billionaire Christopher Harborne, a Thailand-based businessman, who is one of Reform's biggest backers.
Last year he gave a single donation of £9m to Reform - the biggest single donation to a UK political party by a living person.
Creasy was among those who tabled amendments seeking to also impose a cap on UK-based donors.
One of her proposals called for an immediate £500,000 limit which would reduce to £100,000 in the second calendar year. Minsters would have been able to set a permanent cap.
The amendment, which was not moved to a vote, was signed by more than 60 MPs.
Creasy told the Commons: "Obscene wealth is increasingly dictating who is heard, whether we like it or not, what issues are being prioritised and whose interests shape policy decisions."
The Walthamstow MP added that there was a "need to act now to protect the next general election". Her proposals would have exempted trade unions from the donation cap, with the MP saying this is "already well regulated" and "clean money".
Kruger highlighted the millions of pounds donated by trade unions to the Labour Party as he criticised the proposals and the bill.
The MP for East Wiltshire said: "The claim is made that this bill will defend democracy, but actually it's a flagrantly partisan attempt to kneecap Reform UK."
The former Conservative MP added: "The suggestion is made that this bill will restore trust in politics and that is exactly what is needed.
"But what they all mean is to restore trust in the class of politicians and in the political parties that have got us into the mess that we are in, including the party I'm afraid to say I was part of which is why I left it. We need change."
Responding for the government, Eshalomi said the bill "already contains a package of significant measures designed to strengthen the political finance regime whilst ensuring that legitimate donors can continue to fund election campaigns".
The communities minister added that the prime minister was among those "determined to tackle the UK-based issue of mega-donors in UK politics".
"That is why I'm happy to commit and announce the new cross-government task and finish team will be working at pace to find a solution without unintended consequences," Eshalomi said.
"I can reassure members that once these solutions have been found, we would want them in force as soon as possible."
Full details of the new team's remit have yet to be confirmed by the government.
It last month emerged that Burnham registered accepting £345,000 of donations over the past year, including £164,347 from businessman Lord Sainsbury.
The Liberal Democrats proposed establishing a royal commission to make recommendations for a cap on political donations and the "effectiveness" of existing campaign expenditure limits.
This proposal was rejected in the Commons by 427 votes to 85, majority 342.
Green Party MP Ellie Chowns said Creasy had made a "clear case" for a cap on all donations, adding she would prefer it to be lower and suggested £50,000 a year.
Conservative shadow housing secretary Katie Lam said it was a "noble aim" to protect UK democracy from foreign influence but changes proposed by the government had not always been produced with "proper care and attention".
In March, the government said donations in cryptocurrency to UK political parties would be banned alongside the move to cap donations of British citizens living abroad at £100,000 annually.
Ministers later announced overseas voters moving to the UK would be prevented from giving more than £100,000 in political donations for a year after their arrival.
This was announced alongside tougher checks on company donations, which they believe will help stop foreign money from influencing UK elections.
The bill also contains measures to change the voting system, including extending the right to vote to 16- and 17-year-olds.
MPs approved the bill at third reading by 411 votes to 102, majority 309, and it will undergo further scrutiny in the House of Lords at a later date.
results.summary:
The UK government has pledged to establish a task force to address the influence of mega-donors in politics following parliamentary pressure to cap large individual financial contributions.

### Key Points
- Minister Florence Eshalomi confirmed a new cross-government team will work to find solutions for regulating large political donations.
- Labour MP Stella Creasy led calls for a cap, noting that donations of £1 million or more have surged over the last decade.
- Reform UK’s Danny Kruger criticized the proposed Representation of the People Bill as a partisan attempt to limit his party's funding.
- Currently, there are no legal restrictions on the amount of money UK-based individuals or companies can donate to political parties.
- The government has already committed to a £100,000 annual cap on donations from British citizens living overseas.

### Why it Matters
The debate highlights growing concerns regarding the influence of wealthy individuals on policy priorities and the integrity of the UK electoral process. Establishing donation limits could fundamentally reshape political fundraising strategies and alter the financial landscape for all major UK political parties.

results.title: These Sleep Headphones Are My Best Redeye Flight Hack. They Just Got a Nifty Upgrade
results.author: Katie Collins
results.content:
Last month, I took two back-to-back long-haul flights in economy that took me overnight from Asia to the UK. On paper, it sounded like a nightmare, and I was dreading it. But in the end, I managed to get a total of 7 hours of sleep — 5 of them on the first flight, which departed at 2 a.m.
I credit Anker’s Soundcore Sleep A30 earbuds, which drowned out all of the cabin noise around me and were also comfy enough to sleep in. I’ve been searching for this magic combination for a while now, and I finally found it in the A30s.
On Thursday at IFA in Berlin, Anker announced an upgrade to this holy grail product — the Sleep Earbuds 4 and Sleep Earbuds 4 Pro. The company says it’s made the earbuds even smaller, minimizing the 3D ergonomic design for even cozier sleeping. The Sleep 4 Pro also comes with a touchscreen case, allowing you to set alarms, play relaxing sounds and check insights all without touching your phone.
A key feature that sets the Pro model apart from the base model is what Anker calls a “track-assess-adjustment system.” This uses the headphones’ built-in sensors to measure various factors, including PPG, heart rate and HRV and adjust the audio to find the best sleep sounds for you to have the most effective sleep.
The Earbuds 4 will be available in October, with the Earbuds 4 Pro following soon after in November — though pricing is not yet available.
Anker is further building out its sleep ecosystem with a pair of stylish bedside speakers, which it also announced at IFA. The SleepLab will lull you to sleep with soft music and a nightlight, whereas the SleepLap Pro uses radar to track your sleep, heart rate and breathing, then play tailored audio to help you fall asleep and stay asleep — all with no wearables required.
The speakers feature a warm, circular lamp that almost appears to float within a wider cream circle. It looks like a thoughtfully designed piece of kit that I know I’d be happy to have on my bedside table. Anker isn’t sharing pricing or availability at this stage, but says no phone or subscription is required.
Anker headphones and a hearing aid
In May, Anker announced its first neural-net compute-in-memory AI audio chip called Thus, which it’s now put into a slew of new audio products.
The Anker Soundcore AeroClip 2 Pro is more than a pair of clip-on earbuds — the product is actually an AI note-taker that can capture online meetings and calls, transcribing them and providing summaries (not unlike the newly announced Plaud One headphones). There’s no launch date for the AeroClip 2 Pro right now, but there is a price — it will be $230.
Anker is really emphasizing clear call quality in its new audio device lineup. It’s listed as a major selling point of both the over-ear Soundcore Space 2 Pro and the Soundcore Liberty Buds 2. The Space 2 Pro comes with immersive adaptive active noise cancellation and 60 hours of listening time (30 hours with ANC on and 20 hours of talk time). The Libery Buds 2, meanwhile, pack six-sensor full-band ANC, which Anker promises will offer pure silence and block chaos so you can focus fully.
Both models will be available starting Sept. 22, with the Space2 Pro priced at $200 and the Liberty Buds 2 at $130.
The final audio product Anker unveiled at IFA is a little different and won’t be for everyone, but it will prove hugely useful to a select group. The Anker RIC Hearing Aids, also powered by the Thus chip, offer what the company describes as a clinical-grade hearing aid experience.
The device will drown out unnecessary noise and amplify the voice you actually want to hear. Four beamforming microphones will lock onto the voice of the person you’re talking with, and the Thus chip will run 40 billion operations per second to isolate the sound.
There’s no pricing or availability details for the RIC Hearing Aids just yet, but it’s impressive to see Anker use its proprietary tech to develop an accessibility solution. The device will offer 12 hours of battery time, or 36 hours with the case, and 5 minutes of fast charging will give 2 hours of battery life.
Editors’ note: Katie Collins’ travel costs for the IFA conference were covered in part by Xiaomi. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.
results.summary:
Anker unveiled a new lineup of audio products at IFA in Berlin, including upgraded sleep earbuds, AI-powered note-taking devices, and clinical-grade hearing aids featuring proprietary chip technology.

### Key Points
- Anker announced the Sleep Earbuds 4 and 4 Pro, featuring a smaller ergonomic design and a touchscreen case for the Pro model.
- The SleepLab Pro speaker uses radar technology to track sleep, heart rate, and breathing without requiring wearable devices.
- The Soundcore AeroClip 2 Pro, priced at $230, utilizes an AI audio chip to transcribe and summarize meetings and calls.
- New audio hardware, including the $200 Space 2 Pro and $130 Liberty Buds 2, launches on September 22 with advanced noise cancellation.
- The new RIC Hearing Aids use the proprietary Thus chip to perform 40 billion operations per second for real-time voice isolation.

### Why it Matters
Anker is aggressively expanding its audio ecosystem by integrating proprietary AI chips into both consumer electronics and specialized accessibility hardware. This strategy signals a shift toward multifunctional devices that prioritize health tracking and productivity alongside traditional audio performance.

results.title: The Moto Watch Ultra is a return to Wear OS
results.author: Dominic Preston
results.content:
Just a few months after getting back into the smartwatch game, Motorola is targeting the premium end of the market with the first Moto Watch Ultra. It comes with some upgrades from the recent Moto Watch — most obviously the jump to Wear OS — but lacks the outdoorsy features that would make it a true rival to Samsung and Apple’s Ultra watches.
The Moto Watch Ultra is a return to Wear OS
This is a standard smartwatch, and not all that Ultra.
While the Moto Watch ran a custom operating system, Motorola has adopted Google’s Wear OS platform for the Ultra model, with a Snapdragon W5 Plus Gen 1 chip to run it. That gives the Ultra an immediate leg up in terms of access to a wide range of apps, interoperability with the company’s Android phones, and support for NFC payments through Google Wallet. Gemini is supported too, along with Motorola’s own Qira AI assistant.
The downside is battery life. While the Moto Watch boasted an impressive 13 days of runtime, Motorola is only predicting 50 hours of life for the Ultra, and that’s with the always-on display switched off.
At 51g and 12mm thick, the Ultra is a fairly stocky smartwatch, though its 46mm face is actually a little smaller than the normal Moto Watch. Despite that, it actually fits in a larger 1.5-inch OLED display, thanks to a much smaller bezel. The stainless steel body comes in either black or silver, and both ship with a pair of 22mm straps in the box, one silicone and one leather. The silver watch gets green silicone and brown leather, while the black body comes with black, and more black.
The Ultra has an IP68 rating, 5ATM of water-resistance, and Gorilla Glass 3 on the face. Health and fitness tracking is handled through a returning partnership with Polar. It covers heart rate, sleep, stress, SpO2, and recovery, with an AI running coach thrown in too, helped by LTE and dual-band GPS. Still, these aren’t the sort of comprehensive outdoor and extreme sports features you’ll find in the latest Apple Watch Ultra or Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra models, and really this is more in line with those companies’ standard smartwatches.
That’s borne out by the price: The Moto Watch Ultra will cost just $349.99, about half the price of those other Ultras, but a little over double the $149.99 Moto Watch. It’ll be available starting September 10th.

results.title: A breach at Thomson Reuters reached appellate courts in twelve US jurisdictions
results.author: Ana-Maria Stanciuc
results.content:
Thomson Reuters says an unauthorised party got into files belonging to C-Track, the case management platform its court software business sells to judiciaries. The records involved come from appellate courts in a dozen US jurisdictions and from Ontario, Canada.
The company detected the activity in its cloud environment on 30 June, according to Reuters, which is owned by Thomson Reuters. The files were taken in March, three months before anyone noticed.
Public disclosure followed on 2 September, when court systems in several states put out notices on the same day. That is more than five months after the access and more than two after it was found.
The affected jurisdictions named so far are Alabama, Kentucky, Montana, Nevada, New Hampshire, North Dakota, Ohio, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Wyoming and the US Virgin Islands, alongside Ontario. Minnesota’s judicial branch also disclosed an exposure the same week, which would put the count higher than the twelve US jurisdictions in the wire copy.
What sits in those files is the uncomfortable part. Notices sent to court users describe names alongside Social Security numbers, driver’s licence numbers, medical information, dates of birth and health insurance information, and Minnesota warned that some confidential or sealed documents may also have been caught.
Court records are not an ordinary breach target. A case file can contain a protective order, a sealed juvenile matter or a medical filing, which makes the address and phone number attached to it worth considerably more to whoever holds it than the same details lifted from a retailer.
Thomson Reuters says the platform itself kept running. “There has been no operational disruption to C-Track” and “our products and services remain fully operational,” the company said, adding that it brought in outside cybersecurity experts and notified law enforcement.
Individual courts have been blunter. Minnesota Supreme Court Chief Justice Natalie Hudson said she was “deeply troubled that our court users’ data has been compromised,” and Montana Chief Justice Cory Swanson said his courts would keep working with the C-Track team “to ensure our courts operate without fear of compromise of personal privacy.”
Montana learned of the breach on 23 July, six weeks before the public did. The state has told anyone who has been a party to a Montana court case that they may be affected, and has stressed that the data sat on Thomson Reuters servers rather than its own.
Kentucky’s Administrative Office of the Courts said its appellate courts “were not functionally impaired” and that there is “no indication at this point that the unauthorized third party distributed the Kentucky data to any other party or entity.” Its trial courts are untouched because the state does not use an outside vendor for trial court e-filing.
Remediation is running along familiar lines. Thomson Reuters is offering twelve months of credit monitoring and identity theft protection, has stood up a call centre, and system users have been pushed through mandatory password resets.
Nobody has said who was responsible. Reuters reported that it could not independently determine either the attacker or the specifics of what was taken, and no group has publicly claimed the intrusion.
The shape of it is becoming routine. One supplier sits behind dozens of institutions, and a single intrusion reaches all of them at once, which is what happened when an attack on a software vendor rather than a school produced the largest education data breach on record, and again when LastPass customer data was stolen through a supplier.
For Thomson Reuters, which has been rebuilding its engineering organisation around AI, the timing is awkward. Its legal division is the profitable core of the company, and its pitch to courts rests on being the safe place to put a docket.
The count of affected people has not been published. Neither has the mechanism of the intrusion been published, which leaves the twelve jurisdictions describing the same incident in slightly different terms while attacks on US organisations keep shifting in character.

results.title: Face Recognition Is Becoming the Norm for Dating Apps
results.author: Jason Parham
results.content:
In 2025, AI deepfakes flooded Tinder. According to the company, 98 percent of the content-moderation actions on the app were focused on combating fake accounts, scamming, and spam, pushing the company to expand its moderation efforts for its 60 million global users.
The problem is not unique to Tinder. The spread of AI-generated fake accounts has become a rising concern for dating apps, as things like chatfishing and voice cloning have gotten more widespread across the industry.
Among current online daters in the US, nearly half have been targeted by a dating scam, with US romance scams surpassing $4 billion between 2015 and 2025, according to the FBI.
The issue has forced just about every dating platform to adopt stricter authentication tools to ward off scammers. More and more, apps are asking that you surrender your most unique attribute in order to ensure that you’re a real person: your face.
More than a dozen major dating apps and sites use face recognition to verify users, often relying on liveness checks, 3D authentication, video selfies, or biometric ID to demonstrate humanness.
To combat the issue, Tinder launched the mandatory face-screening tool Face Check for new members in October 2025. “It’s not a feature. It’s a statement about what human connection online should require,” Yoel Roth, head of trust and safety for Match Group, which owns Tinder, said to WIRED in an email. Match Group tells WIRED that it is also starting to require Face Check for existing users in several of Tinder’s core markets, including the US and UK.
As face verification slowly transforms into a prerequisite for participation across the industry, the collective drive to combat bad actors has created a necessary and equally concerning new standard where “proof of human” profiles may soon be the norm.
Underpinning the shift, however, is a grim irony: In attempting to solve the problem of knowing whether someone is real, Big Dating is potentially creating more opportunities for privacy and security risks by forcing users to give up biometric data, while also legitimizing a culture of surveillance.
One company pushing for the use of ID-verification tech in dating apps is Tools for Humanity. The AI company created World ID, an iris-scanning biometric verification system, and partnered with Tinder in April, though it’s still optional for users. The most distinct feature about World ID is that confirmed users receive a “verified human” badge on the app after undergoing the process, which requires them to scan the colored part of their eye using the company’s orb device. They are given an identification number as their official World ID.
“In the near future, any dating app, like most online platforms in general, will need some sort of proof-of-human system like this,” says Tiago Sada, chief product officer at Tools for Humanity, adding that the way the majority of dating platforms handle verification is “super creepy, because you have to give your personal data to every single app that you want to use.” As stipulated by World’s policy, the orb does not share or retain any data; it is able to verify users without ever sending their data to a server. Once your image is confirmed, the orb sends the coded image to your phone before permanently deleting it, the company claims. Likewise, Face Check collects and stores an encrypted map of information about the shape of the user’s face, not the actual picture, Match said.
But even as dating apps claim that your biometric data is safe, security continues to be a significant concern.
Dating apps are subject to occasional data breaches, and while the inherent premise in these ID systems is that verification equals trust, cybersecurity researcher Katie Moussouris says that they are mostly a smoke screen. “Normalizing the idea that a face scan provides any assurance of identity or age is security theater.”
A liveness check requiring face scanning and live video only indicates a person was present at sign-up and does not guarantee that the person was not using AI to alter their appearance in real time. Likewise, an ID scan indicates an ID was presented, not that it belongs to the person who presented it. “Neither should be confused with trust,” Moussouris says. “A verified profile can still belong to a romance scammer who took over an account or created one using AI tools.”
And while passwords and usernames are interchangeable, faces are not, which makes them unique targets for attacks. More than that, biometric verification sets a risky precedent, says Woodrow Hartzog, a technology law professor at Boston University who previously served on the Massachusetts special commission on facial recognition.
“When we get accustomed to having our face scanned for everything we do online, it is really dangerous, not only potentially for the privacy risks but also to acclimate an entire population into thinking that that is normal behavior,” he says. “Facial recognition is the most dangerous surveillance tool ever created.”
Existing privacy laws are not equipped to deal with biometric verification on dating apps, according to Hartzog. He believes policies should ensure that less invasive options are used when they're available. In the case of biometrics, for example, your face, which can be monitored everywhere you go, is much more dangerous to collect than your thumbprint.
Utah’s State-Endorsed Digital Identity law, which went into effect in May, was one of the first major attempts at that. It limits the kinds of data that can be requested to only what is absolutely necessary while establishing a “duty of loyalty,” meaning platforms and providers cannot engage in practices that “conflict with the best interests of an individual” or “result in a disproportionate risk” to them. The law attempts to mitigate situations where people might have to present ID every time they log online, and also includes significant rules on the entity that’s collecting the data. The American Civil Liberties Union called it “the nation’s strongest digital identity bill.”
“Look at how easy it is to channel people's choices into agreeing to have their faces scanned as a condition of a good or service,” Hartzog says. “The more we can lean into policy frameworks that require strong protections from the company—rather than putting the onus on the person whose face is being scanned or who has to reveal their identity—then the better off I think we’ll be.”
results.summary:
Tinder and other major dating platforms are mandating biometric face-scanning tools to combat a surge in AI-generated deepfakes, romance scams, and fraudulent accounts affecting millions of users.

### Key Points
- Tinder launched mandatory "Face Check" verification for new members in October 2025, with plans to expand the requirement to existing users in the US and UK.
- FBI data indicates that US romance scams resulted in over $4 billion in losses between 2015 and 2025.
- More than a dozen dating apps now utilize 3D authentication, liveness checks, or video selfies to verify user identities.
- Tools for Humanity partnered with Tinder in April to offer optional iris-scanning verification through its "World ID" system.
- Utah’s Digital Identity law, effective May 2025, establishes a "duty of loyalty" to limit data collection and protect user privacy against invasive surveillance practices.

### Why it Matters
The shift toward biometric verification creates a new industry standard that prioritizes security but raises significant concerns regarding long-term privacy and the normalization of mass surveillance. While these tools aim to reduce fraud, experts warn that biometric data is uniquely vulnerable and that "proof of human" systems may offer a false sense of security against sophisticated AI actors.

results.title: Utah becomes the first US state to target VPNs with a strict age verification law, but top providers refuse to budge
results.author: chiara.castro@futurenet.com (Chiara Castro) , Chiara Castro
results.content:
- Utah’s SB 73 takes effect today, September 3, but ongoing legal challenges mean strict enforcement could remain paused.
- Anyone physically in Utah is legally treated as a resident, even if they use a VPN to mask their location, and websites face a $2,500 penalty per violation.
- Leading VPN providers confirm they will not change how their services operate in Utah, calling the legislation a "dangerous precedent" that fails to solve age assurance.
Utah has become ground zero for a major digital rights battle. Following months of intense legal wrangling, Utah’s Senate Bill 73 (SB 73) comes into effect today, September 3.
Originally scheduled for a May rollout, the law was temporarily paused following a court injunction. That initial pause has now expired, allowing the law to come into effect and making Utah the first US state to explicitly target VPN use for age verification mandates.
But the cybersecurity industry is warning that the legislation remains a convoluted, unenforceable mess.
As reported by Gizmodo, SB 73, formally known as the Online Age Verification Amendments, requires commercial websites hosting adult material to verify user ages.
The privacy concerns lie in how the state handles location spoofing: anyone physically located in Utah is legally treated as a Utah user, regardless of the IP address they present to a website.
This means if a resident of Salt Lake City connects to a VPN server in Germany, they are still a Utah user in the eyes of the law, and the website remains legally liable for verifying their age. If websites fail to comply, they face severe penalties reaching $2,500 per violation.

A "dangerous precedent" for privacy tools
To comply with the law, websites may be forced to use highly intrusive tracking measures or block all suspected VPN traffic. Furthermore, adult websites are now legally barred from publishing instructions on how to use a VPN to circumvent the state's age gates.
Digital rights groups have previously slammed the framework as an "impossible by design" waste of money that simply creates a technical whack-a-mole. This legislative push isn't happening in a vacuum, as authorities globally, including the EU, increasingly view VPNs as circumvention software that needs to be restricted.
However, some of the best VPNs are refusing to alter their services for Utah residents, noting that the legal burden falls entirely on website operators.
Speaking exclusively to TechRadar, Laura Tyrylyte, privacy advocate at NordVPN, clarified that the September 3 rollout is far from final. "The legal challenge to the law is still ongoing, so September 3 should not be treated as a set enforcement date. Depending on how things move, enforcement could remain paused while litigation continues," Tyrylyte explained.
"That said, SB 73 does not affect NordVPN directly as the law's obligations fall on websites that host content deemed harmful to minors, not on VPN providers," she continued. "However, the trend of rushed-out laws that are impossible to comply with is far from reassuring, and we will continue to advocate for approaches to child safety that don't sacrifice the cybersecurity and privacy tools that protect everyone."
AdGuard VPN has taken a similar stance. Denis Vyazovoy, Head of Products at AdGuard, confirmed to TechRadar that the company has no intention of restricting its local users.
“We don’t currently see Utah’s SB 73 as creating direct compliance obligations for VPN providers, so we don’t plan to change how AdGuard VPN works for users in Utah," Vyazovoy said. "More broadly, treating VPNs as a loophole in age-verification policy sets a dangerous precedent: VPNs are general-purpose privacy and security tools, and restricting them risks harming legitimate users without solving the underlying problem of age assurance.”
Gytis Malinauskas, Head of Legal at Surfshark, told TechRadar that Utah's SB 73 sets a concerning precedent. "In practice, it requires sites that host content deemed harmful to minors to block VPNs. This treats a core cybersecurity tool as a loophole. VPNs are a standard security tool millions of Americans use every day to protect their data. Blocking them would only erode the privacy of ordinary users," he said.
For now, everyday encryption remains completely legal in Utah. However, as the burden of proof shifts to website operators, users can expect to face significantly more invasive identity checks, or blanket blocklists, as companies attempt to navigate the new state rules.

results.title: How to Learn Fast — and Kill Weak Bets Early
results.author: Braden Kelley
results.content:
The Experiment Canvas™: Five Gravity-Control Innovation Experiments Visualized
by Braden Kelley and Art Inteligencia
What Is The Experiment Canvas™? (Short Answer)
The Experiment Canvas™ is a one-page innovation tool for structuring experiments that prove or disprove the feasibility, viability, and desirability of a potential innovation — before you burn capital on the wrong bet. It forces a clear hypothesis, helpers, resources, risks, assumptions, barriers, a three-phase experiment plan (setup → execution → wrap-up), and learning metrics that can falsify the idea.
Below: why the canvas accelerates innovation speed and success rates — and five filled examples for a hypothetical gravity control appliance, showing how a radical idea can be broken into sequenced experiments that cull likely failures early.
Why Innovators Need to Instrument for Learning — Not Hope
Most innovation waste is not bad imagination. It is unfalsified imagination: teams fund prototypes, labs, and roadmaps without a written hypothesis, kill criteria, or a learning metric anyone would defend in a budget meeting. Activity photographs well. Learning does not — unless you design for it.
I created The Experiment Canvas™ as part of the Human-Centered Innovation Toolkit™ to help teams instrument for learning fast in iterative new product or service development. The canvas makes the experiment visual and collaborative — so alignment, accountability, and outcomes improve together. Specs can follow. Hope should not lead.
Used well, the canvas helps you:
- Accelerate speed — by sequencing the questions that matter (physics before scale; safety before market theater; cost before Series B fantasy).
- Raise odds of success — by naming helpers, resources, assumptions, and barriers before the first dollar of build.
- Cull likely failures early — with fail-fast gates and learning metrics that can say “no” while the bet is still cheap.
How The Experiment Canvas™ Structures a Bet
Each canvas asks the same disciplined questions, in roughly this flow:
| Zone | What it forces | 
|---|---|
| Hypothesis | The question, feasibility/viability/desirability angles, fatal flaws, adoption blockers | 
| Who can help / resources / risks | Real people, real tools, real downside — not a slide of optimism | 
| Phases 1–3 | Setup, execution, wrap-up with evidence, insight, and next gate | 
| Assumptions & barriers | What must be true — and what can stop you | 
| Learning metrics | Three measures that can falsify the bet | 
To show how this works on something intentionally extreme, I recently built five Experiment Canvas examples (CLICK THEM to get the big version) for a hypothetical gravity control appliance. The point is not sci-fi cosplay. The point is method: even a moonshot becomes manageable when you break it into experiments that can fail honestly.
Example 1 — Physics Feasibility: Is There Any Measurable Effect?
Core hypothesis: Can we create >0.1% weight reduction on a 1kg mass — or is there any measurable effect at all?
This first canvas attacks the fatal question: is there a signal, or are we chasing EMI / magnetic tricks and reputational risk? Helpers include a chief scientist, a gravimetry lab, metrology, and an external skeptic reviewer. Learning metrics demand delta-G, signal-to-noise (>3 sigma), and repeatability. Next gate: if yes → energy test; if no → pivot or kill.
Example 2 — Energy Efficiency: Is the Cost Per Newton Survivable?
Core hypothesis: Can we achieve >1 Newton of lift per kW — and modulate ±2% for 60 seconds — without an energy cost that makes the product impossible?
Prerequisite: Example 1 success. This canvas puts power electronics, thermal management, and fail-fast gates on the page (>5 kW/N kills the path). Metrics: watts per Newton, modulation accuracy, thermal stability. Insight: is the curve linear — or a cliff? Soft landings for radical tech start with honesty about energy economics.
Example 3 — Safety Envelope: Is Exposure Safe Enough to Sell?
Core hypothesis: Is 8-hour exposure at 0.5G at 1 meter safe — for cells, electronics, and humans?
Prerequisite: a stable Example 2. Here feasibility, desirability, and viability collide: bio impact, EMC, nausea, regulatory classification, liability. Metrics include cell viability (>95% vs control), bit-error rate / EMC compliance, and human symptom reports. Next: define a safety manual and exclusion zone — or stop before market theater begins.
Example 4 — Market Desirability: Who Has Gravity Pain Worth Paying For?
Core hypothesis: Which segment has ~$10M gravity-related pain — and will they sign LOIs at real price points ($120k+ / $520k+), or is this cool tech nobody wants?
Prerequisite: safety envelope from Example 3. This is the desirability canvas — interviews, pain scores, willingness to pay, and traction via pilot LOIs. Done when you have enough contact evidence for a go or a clear no-go. Building without a segment that hurts is innovation theater with better physics.
Example 5 — Manufacturing Viability: Can We Build 10 Betas Under $50k BOM?
Core hypothesis: Can we build 10 beta units at under $50k bill of materials — with a real path through supply chain, yield, and compliance?
This viability canvas asks whether the existing supply chain works, whether FCC/OSHA/product safety is a path or a wall, and whether cost or yield kills margin. Fail fast if BOM exceeds $100k. Metrics: unit cost, manufacturability (yield and hours), compliance blockers. Next: if cost and path are clear → fund the next round; if not → redesign before you scale a fantasy.
What These Five Canvases Teach About Speed and Success
Read the five examples in sequence and a pattern appears:
- Sequence the fatal questions. Physics before energy. Energy before safety. Safety before market. Market before manufacturing scale.
- Write the kill criteria in advance. Null result, >5 kW/N, unsafe exposure, no LOIs, BOM blowout — each canvas names how to stop.
- Make learning metrics falsifiable. Three metrics per canvas beat a hundred vanity KPIs.
- Surface helpers, risks, assumptions, and barriers. Innovation fails politically as often as it fails scientifically.
- Treat wrap-up as a decision, not a report. Evidence → insight → next gate. No cemetery of unfinished experiments.
You do not need a gravity appliance to use the method. You need a bet you are tempted to fund on enthusiasm alone — and the discipline to instrument learning before the money gets loud.

If you think compact discs are a thing of the past, you probably haven’t been around a K-pop fan or a hoarder who still has their CDs from decades ago. Then there are people like me who have a stack of CDs collected over the years but no actual CD player to enjoy them on, since options that are strong on both quality and design are hard to come by.
The ClearFrame Speaker CD Player is a solid choice for anyone looking for a visually stunning player that won’t let a CD’s album art go to waste. It lets you slot the jacket art onto the front of the player so it becomes a rotating piece of wall or shelf art. Or, if you’d rather show off the mechanics, you can leave the artwork out and display the transparent body itself, watching your CD spin with all its moving (and non-moving) parts in full view.
Whenever I come across beautiful album art, I can’t help but think it’s wasted if it only ever gets seen as a tiny digital thumbnail on a streaming app. A player like the ClearFrame Speaker CD Player lets you put that kind of artwork on full display while you’re enjoying the music in your room. Seeing something that the artist, and the album art designer, worked hard on come to life while it spins gives it the justice it deserves. And if you’d rather see the clear, polycarbonate-style body become a piece of art in its own right, just take out the album cover and let it shine in all its transparent glory.
This is also an upgraded version of the original, and already popular, ClearFrame CD Player, since it now comes with a built-in speaker. That means you no longer need to hook it up to an external Bluetooth speaker or wired setup, which makes it even more flexible to display anywhere in your home. You actually have three ways to listen to your favorite CDs: through the built-in 40mm speaker, with wired headphones through the 3.5mm jack, or over Bluetooth 5.3 to external speakers or headphones if you already have a better setup you’d like to use.
Beyond the listening options, the ClearFrame Speaker CD Player was clearly designed with portability in mind. At just 454 grams (about a pound) and roughly the size of a hardcover book, it’s light enough to carry from your bedroom to your living room without a second thought. Its 1,800mAh battery gives you around six to seven hours of playback through the built-in speaker, or seven to eight hours if you’re streaming over Bluetooth, so you can enjoy a few albums back-to-back before needing to recharge via USB-C. There’s even a retro-style LED Nixie tube display that adds a warm, nostalgic touch to the whole experience, plus a 2MB SDRAM anti-shock buffer so accidental bumps won’t make your music skip.
For collectors, this player also solves a real problem: what to do with all the CDs sitting untouched in a drawer somewhere. Instead of treating them like outdated clutter, the ClearFrame gives them a reason to come back out, whether that’s a K-pop photocard-era album, a mix your best friend burned for you in high school, or a boxed set you’ve been meaning to revisit. It turns “old technology” into a genuine decor piece you’d be proud to leave out on a shelf.
If you’re looking to gift this to someone (or, let’s be honest, treat yourself), the ClearFrame Speaker CD Player comes in a few configurations depending on how you plan to display it. You can pick it up on its own, or add a wall mount, book case, or display stand, so it fits neatly into whatever corner of your home you have in mind. It isn’t the cheapest CD player on the market, but if you have a stack of CDs with nowhere to go and album art too good to keep hidden, this one earns its price tag by turning something you already own into something worth looking at every single day.

The ClearFrame Speaker CD Player combines nostalgic physical media playback with modern design, allowing users to display album art while listening through a built-in speaker or Bluetooth connectivity.

### Key Points
- The device features a transparent polycarbonate body and a slot to display physical album artwork as a rotating piece of home decor.
- It includes a built-in 40mm speaker, a 3.5mm headphone jack, and Bluetooth 5.3 support for versatile audio output.
- The unit weighs 454 grams and is powered by an 1,800mAh battery, providing up to eight hours of playback per charge via USB-C.
- Integrated hardware includes a retro-style LED Nixie tube display and a 2MB SDRAM anti-shock buffer to prevent playback skipping.
- Optional accessories include a wall mount, book case, and display stand to accommodate various home interior configurations.

### Why it Matters
This device addresses the growing demand for physical media among collectors by transforming outdated CD collections into functional, aesthetic home decor. By integrating modern wireless features into a portable design, it bridges the gap between vintage music formats and contemporary lifestyle preferences.

results.title: As millions of kids lose SNAP food benefits, free school meals are also at risk
results.author: Juliana Kim
results.content:
As millions of kids lose SNAP food benefits, free school meals are also at risk
When Republican lawmakers secured cuts to the United States' largest food assistance program last year, Paige Shoemaker DeMio wasn't worried about children going hungry just at home — but at school.
"Anytime we're hearing about cuts to SNAP or Medicaid, we're worried about what's going to be the domino effect of this," she says.
Shoemaker DeMio is a senior policy analyst at the Center for American Progress, a left-leaning think tank. She usually focuses on K-12 education, but in recent months, she has been following the changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, also known as SNAP or food stamps.
That's because SNAP connects children with other critical resources, such as free breakfast and lunch at school. So when a family loses access to food assistance, the family's child may stop automatically receiving free food at school. And when scores of families fall off SNAP, universal free meal programs at tens of thousands of schools fall into jeopardy.
The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities estimates that over a million children have lost food benefits since July 2025, when the One Big Beautiful Bill Act was signed into law. Among the changes, the legislation led to stricter work requirements to receive food assistance.
Going into this academic year, dozens of schools nationwide have ended their universal free meal programs — including schools in San Antonio, Houston and Miami-Dade County. School nutrition experts say it's unclear to what extent a decline in SNAP participation played a role. But Diane Pratt-Heavner, a spokesperson for the School Nutrition Association, which represents about 50,000 school nutrition professionals in the U.S., says that the full impact on free school meals will emerge in the coming years as SNAP changes take effect.
"This moment in time could potentially be a tip-of-an-iceberg situation," she says "It could get much, much worse."
In a statement, the U.S. Agriculture Department, which administers SNAP and school meals on the federal level, said it invests $385 million for low-income communities and people in need of nutrition assistance.
"School meal programs have varying income limits, and while SNAP participation may ease the application process, a family not on SNAP is not automatically disallowed participation," the department stated.
School districts will have to reassess whether they can afford free meals
The Agriculture Department's Community Eligibility Provision helps pay for universal free meals at a school or district if at least a quarter of students participate in assistance programs like SNAP. (If it's 62.5% or more, the federal government covers the full tab.) More than 49,000 public schools participated as of the 2024-2025 school year, according to the Center for American Progress.
Federal reimbursement fluctuates based on the percentage of families receiving assistance. A decline in food stamp participation can lead to a decrease in federal funding, forcing schools to pay more for universal free food when their budgets are already stretched thin, according to Pratt-Heavner.
This could push schools to shift funds away from classroom needs or decide to stop offering universal free meals altogether, she adds. If districts decide to do away with their free food programs, they may still incur costs in the form of debt from unpaid meals.
That's what happened in 2023. When the U.S. ended a federal pandemic waiver allowing schools nationwide to offer free meals, districts reported accruing meal debt as high as $1.7 million, according to a report by the School Nutrition Association.
"Unpaid meal debt becomes an issue not only for the school meal program, but for the school district budget, which has to pay teachers and for textbooks," Pratt-Heavner says. "It's just a no-win situation for anyone."
Erin Bronner is the director of child nutrition and wellness for a small school district in central Phoenix that participates in the Community Eligibility Provision (CEP). Arizona has seen the most dramatic decline in SNAP participation in the country, with more than 400,000 people — including about 180,000 children — losing food assistance over the past year.
Now, Bronner's district is due to reapply for the provision next year. She says she's worried whether her district can afford to keep offering universal free meals.
"Due to the dramatic decline in SNAP assistance, the percentage of eligible families [is] not high enough for us to be able to financially sustain operating this provision," she says. "So we would actually lose money if we were to continue to operate CEP."
The kids in the "danger zone"
Students qualify for free food at school if their family earns at or below 130% of the poverty line, which is $42,900 for a family of four in 2026. Reduced-price meals are offered to such families making $61,050 or less.
To access free or reduced-price meals, students can fill out a school meal application. But the form tends to be a source of confusion and administrative burden, according to Shoemaker DeMio.
"It's easier and faster for children to get fed when meals are universally given rather than individually applied for," she says.
Another issue with the application is that it factors in only income and doesn't take into account a family's expenses or unique hardships, according to Pratt-Heavner. There are no exceptions or waivers.
"So, a family that's struggling with a recent rent increase or has a family [member] undergoing cancer treatment may be spending more than they're taking in and might not be eligible for any help at all," she says.
Bronner, in Arizona, calls it the "danger zone": when a student's family makes just above the income threshold but is still cash-strapped.
"They do fall through the cracks," she says. "And because of where they fall income-wise, it doesn't leave us too many options to try and provide an alternative for them."
School policy experts say they're also concerned for children of noncitizens, even though free or reduced-price meals are available to all students regardless of immigration status. They're concerned because such children's parents may be afraid to share personal information in the school meal application — such as the last four digits of their Social Security number — amid a nationwide immigration crackdown.
Losing access to free meals could require families to spend on average nearly $1,000 per student each school year, according to the Center for American Progress. Shoemaker DeMio says that cost burden comes as many families are already grappling with high living costs and steep gas prices.
" That's a lot of money," she says. "Especially when we're talking about these families who are on the cusp of eligibility and who are also facing an affordability crisis."
Concerns about growing hunger
Currently, nine states offer permanent universal free school meals: California, Colorado, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Mexico, New York and Vermont. In recent years, other states have introduced legislation to move toward this direction.
But those universal free meal programs also have been a topic of debate. Opponents say that they're costly and that the government shouldn't pay for students whose families can afford school meals. Meanwhile, advocates argue that school meals tend to be healthier and promote better education outcomes.
" Schools provide books, they provide pencils, they even provide laptops these days to help students be ready to learn, and nutrition is no different," Shoemaker DeMio says. " Nutrition is a foundational ingredient to student success."
Sharon Glosson, the executive director of school nutrition at North East Independent School District in San Antonio, supports universal free school meals. Glosson says she has seen it remove stigma and shame for low-income students in the lunch line.
" It's open to everyone, and there's no differentiation between those that qualify for free and reduced price and those that don't," she says.
But this school year, her district announced that it would have to stop offering universal free meals at nearly half its campuses. Glosson believes the biggest factor was a decline in the number of families receiving food assistance — though the need to help ease hunger is still there.
"We know that within our families in our school district, their economic status between now and four years ago, they don't feel that it has improved to the point where they are now able to pay for school meals," she says.
results.summary:
Millions of children are losing access to free school meals as stricter SNAP eligibility requirements under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act reduce federal funding for school districts.

### Key Points
- Over one million children have lost SNAP food benefits since the July 2025 enactment of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
- The Community Eligibility Provision (CEP) allows schools to offer universal free meals if a sufficient percentage of students participate in SNAP.
- Declining SNAP enrollment is forcing districts in cities like San Antonio, Houston, and Miami-Dade to end universal free meal programs.
- Families earning just above the federal poverty threshold often fall into a "danger zone" where they struggle to afford meals but do not qualify for assistance.
- Nine states, including California and New York, currently maintain permanent universal free school meal programs despite federal funding fluctuations.

### Why it Matters
The reduction in SNAP participation creates a significant financial burden for school districts, which must choose between absorbing meal debt or cutting other educational resources. This shift threatens to increase food insecurity for vulnerable students and may force families to spend nearly $1,000 annually per child on school lunches.
